Section 5 shows the empirical experiment and results, and Section 6 gives the conclusion and further discussion.\\
\section[Related works of Chapter 2]{Related works}\label{sec:related works}
Before \citet{Treynor1961MarketRisk} created the CAPM model, people had fuzzy notions about how the risks could affect the expected returns of assets. He proposed a single-factor linear model for interpreting expected stock returns via a factor generated from the difference between expected market return and the risk-free rate. Specifically, it can be written as:
\begin{equation}
E(R_i) = R_f + \beta_i \left(E(R_m) - R_f\right)
\end{equation}
Where $E(R_i)$ is the expected return of asset $i$, $R_f$ is the risk-free rate, $\beta_i$ is the asset's beta, representing its sensitivity to the market, and $E(R_m)$ is the expected return of the market. Although it is the cornerstone of the asset pricing theory, people cast doubts on the explainability of the market factor to the individual assets or portfolios. Thus, \citet{Ross1978TheCAPM} reckoned asset returns were driven by the combined effect of factors, hence proposed a generalized factor model’s frame:
\begin{equation}
R_i = \alpha_i + \beta_{i1} F_1 + \beta_{i2} F_2 + \cdots + \beta_{ik} F_k + \epsilon_i
\end{equation}
Where $F_1$ to $F_k$ are factors, $\beta_{i1}$ to $\beta_{ik}$ are coefficients which measure the sensitivity of the factors, also known as factor loadings. $\alpha_i$ is the intercept of the linear model, it can be interpreted as a pricing error, and the residual $\epsilon_i$ can present the firm-specific risks. This theory suggests that if the pricing mismatches the factors’ offers, investors can take advantage of the arbitrage. It is known as Arbitrage Pricing Theory (APT). The profit from the arbitrage is equal to $\alpha_i$ which is that the returns cannot be explained fully by the factors. The model frame released the single-factor assumption from CAPM, hence, it increased the flexibility of the model. However, with such a frame, scholars still struggle with questions such as what factors should be present and how many factors should appear in a single frame. The most well-known multi-factor model is the Fama-French 3-factor model (FF3) \citep{Fama1993CommonBonds}. It deployed the market factor together with size and value (book-to-market ratio) factors to the APT frame, which  improved the explanation of the sorted portfolios. The FF3 model led to an increased enthusiasm for research on factor exploration afterwards. Researchers developed new factors and models based on the APT frame and had the massive competition competed models on the their interpretability factors and their combinations’ interpretability which normally presented as the higher coefficient of determination and insignificant value of $\alpha$. For example, \citet{Carhart1997OnPerformance} extended FF3 to 4 factors by adding the momentum factor, while \citet{Novy-Marx2013ThePremium} proposed adding a gross profit factor to the FF3 frame. Further development led to the Fama French 5 factor (FF5) model \citep{Fama2015AModel} which added profitability and investment factors to FF3.  \citet{Hou2015DigestingApproach} optimized the FF5’s investment factor by Tobin's Q theory \citep{Tobin1969ATheory} which utilized the ratio of the market value of the company and replaced the cost of capital to measure the quality of investment. They offered great ideas on how to interpret asset or portfolio returns. However, with continuously emerging new factors and countless combinations brought by these factors, it remains a key research challenge to assess the reliability of different factors. There are four hundred plus factors which play a role in stock pricing \citep{Hou2020ReplicatingAnomalies}. Handpicking factors may cause the ‘omitted variable’ issue, which means important variables are neglected intentionally or unintentionally. However, inserting all factors in the APT frame causes the ‘dimensionality disaster’ since it leads to the heavy multicollinearity issue of the linear APT frame, which lowers the interpretability of the factors. \\ 

Therefore, a branch of the researchers devotes themselves to developing non-linear model forms or adding constraints to the linear form to satisfy the increasing factor size. \citet{Stock2002ForecastingPredictors} introduced the use of principal components analysis (PCA) to subtract factors from a large dimension of predictors. PCA projects the predictors into the new coordinate system via a linear transformation and reorganizes the predictors into components. It subtracts components which have the highest explanation for the variance as the new factors for the APT frame. The entire process is named principal components regression (PCR), and the pre-defined parameter which indicates how many new factors should be taken is known as the hyperparameter of PCR. PCA is the most widely applied technique for dimension reduction tasks, but it has limitations as the linear assumption of predictors, new factors generated based on a linear combination of the original predictors may not be easy to interpret and require normalization. Later, \citet{Kelly2019CharacteristicsReturn} utilized the incremental PCA (IPCA) which upgraded from the PCA for predictor abstracting. IPCA employed a dynamic process on PCA, which only analyses a small batch of the entire dataset each time and updates the new factors gradually, ultimately approaching the optimum factors for the full dataset. Although IPCA improved the quality of new factors, the shortcomings of the PCA persist in IPCA. \\

Furthermore, the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) known as $l1$ penalty and ridge regression known as $l2$ penalty as two commonly applied constrains for linear models. They are employed for controlling the oversized predictors. \citet{Kelly2013MarketValues} proposed a new pricing method via market expectation which relies on LASSO for noise reduction.  \citet{Feng2020TamingFactors} introduced the concept of ‘factor zoo’ and an applied LASSO-based examination method. \citet{Chinco2019SparseReturns} has also verified LASSO’s ability to denoise datasets. They proved that LASSO regression can significantly reduce the noise created by ineffective factors and improve model fitness and robustness. Whereas the classic LASSO has limitations such as subtracting only one factor from a group of highly correlated factors, its limitation is that it cannot jointly measure multiple correlated or equally important factors. This leads to information loss. Therefore, some papers turn to the constraint of classic ridge regression. For example, \citet{Giglio2021AssetFactors} applied ridge regression to the study of how investor beliefs have an impact on portfolio decisions from a survey of wealthy retail investors. It matched the survey data to investors' portfolios, trading activities, and online behaviors data. It proved that the $l2$ penalty can identify which factors should be the prioritized factors, identifying potential multicollinearity and moderating model overfitting in the dataset. Nonetheless, classic ridge regression has limitations such as it is impossible to eliminate the ineffective factors since it never fails to shrink the coefficients to zero, and it penalizes all correlated factors when it addresses the multicollinearity, which makes it difficult to interpret the individual effect of factors with high correlation. Moreover, for sparse factors, where only a few variables have significant effects, ridge regression shows less priority than LASSO due to the effect of non-zero coefficient shrinkage. Both classic LASSO and ridge regression face the same limitations of being computationally expensive and time-consuming for searching hyperparameters and are therefore not suitable for non-linear data and are sensitive to noises. \citet{Yuan2006ModelVariables,Freyberger2020DissectingNonparametrically,Bertelsen2022TheZoo} later extended LASSO to group LASSO, adaptive group LASSO and prior adaptive LASSO respectively, for moderating the aforementioned issues of classic LASSO, but it still has not been fundamentally resolved. \\

Fortunately, the development of machine learning (ML) has led to the progression of the factor model’s frame exploration. The earliest neural network (NN) models for financial application can be traced back to the 1990s, where \citet{Hutchinson1994ANetworks} used a new non-parametric NN model for simulating Black-Scholes option price. They proved that the model recovered the Black-Scholes formula from a two-year training set of daily options prices, and it can be used on both out-of-sample price and delta-hedge options, which gave hope to later research that NN models may conquer some limitations of traditional econometric methods. Later, \citet{Heaton2016DeepFinance} tested classic deep NN structures on financial time series prediction tasks, from MLP to Autoencoder, and found deep neural network structures significantly  improved the performance of financial series prediction. \citet{Gu2020EmpiricalLearning} examined the classic ML methods, including MLP, decision tree and random forest, on 30,000 US stocks for 60 years. They found MLP with 3-4 hidden layers outperform all other models by comparing the average out-of-sample (OOS) fitness indicator $R^2$. Their models in later works are also named ‘GKX2020’ \citet{Gu2021AutoencoderModels}. Rresearch in this chapter has developed from \citet{Gu2021AutoencoderModels}'s MLP models. By following their footpath, \citet{Wang2021CryptocurrenciesLearning} deployed their methods on the cryptocurrencies and found similar results. \citet{Giglio2021AssetFactors} solved the omitted variables issue of the asset pricing factor model by proposing an innovative ML model for dimensional reduction tasks. More advanced, \citet{Gu2021AutoencoderModels} extended the idea from IPCA, which developed an autoencoder model for the dimension reduction. Adopting an autoencoder structure in factor models can be seen as a generalized PCA model which has the capability to relax the linearity assumption between original factors. \citet{Avramov2021MachinePredictability} did comparative research for previous ML on factor models, where they demonstrated ML methods can consistently identify mispriced stocks and handle the anomalies better, albeit acknowledging the black-box effect of ML models. Also, they indicated that the trading signals generated by deep learning methods are more profitable, especially for long positions. Moreover, the deep learning methods moderated downside risk significantly. \citet{Giglio2022FactorPricing} did a comprehensive literature review on ML-based asset pricing research. They concluded that although ML assisted in improving the model performance, pure ML techniques are far from solving the asset pricing assignment, and researchers should consider exploring the economic and financial meanings behind models. They also suggested that macroeconomic and microeconomic activities should be adopted. \citet{Kelly2023FinancialLearning} contributed a more general literature review in ML for the financial application domain. They mentioned that ML for finance is already extended to the speech and textual recognition fields, and it could be exciting for the attempt at corporate finance research. More theoretically, \citet{Chen2019EmpiricalStrategy} used Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) for searching the most appropriate function form for the stochastic discount factor (SGD) of factor models. It is the seminal paper on the application of advanced models such as GAN in the asset pricing domain which triggered the initial interest in the GAN and its variation in factor models \citet{Wang2024RVRAE:Prediction}. \citet{Eckerli2021GenerativeOverview} overviewed the recent development of GAN-based models in financial applications. Practically, \citet{Coqueret2020MachineVersion} discussed the implementation of traditional ML models such as random forest, MLP, autoencoder and reinforcement learning for factor investing trading strategy designing. It also provided examples with R codes. \citet{Dixon2020MachinePractice} well matched the two angles for ML: theory and practice, providing the mechanism presentation and implementation in general financial application. It introduced the classic ML models and how they accommodate tasks such as decision-making and sequential learning. \\
\section[Data Description of Chapter 2]{Data Description}\label{sec:Data Description} 
The responses, or labels in ML terminology, used in this research contain 420 large-capital stock excess returns from January 1957 to December 2021. These stocks come from the US NASDAQ and NYSE markets which are derived from CRSP of Wharton Research Data Services (WRDS). These 420 stocks originally are filtered from the top 15\% of the largest market capital (MC) which covers 85\% of total MC for the two markets. They satisfy the conditions of having no missing data in the testing period  and less than 50\% of values missing during the training period, so it can meet the requirement of the ‘going concern’ \citep{Fama1970EfficientMarkets} and data representability. As a benefit of the assumption of ‘too-big-to-fail’ \citep{Mishkin2006HowBailouts} and ‘going concern’ , this setting is more realistic for practitioners since it protects the investors from systematic risks such as companies who delisted unexpectedly due to insolvency (e.g. Lehman Brothers). The overall coverage of market capital from these stocks is 21.38\% in the US stock markets of National Association of Securities Dealers Automated Quotations (NASDAQ) and the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE). The risk-free rate for constructing the excess returns and evaluating the Sharp ratio (SR) and Sortino ratio (SO) are derived from the Kenneth R. French Data Library. \\

The predictors, also known as features for the ML terminology, organized by 182 explored firm characteristic sorted portfolio factors from asset pricing literature offered by \citet{AndrewY.Zimmermann2020OpenPricing} with at least 60\% of available values in the training period. The entire data set is split into training, validation and testing periods as shown in Table~\ref{tab:data_split}. The training window is on an extension base with a step size of 12 months, while the validation window is fixed with 119 observations.  The training window together with a fixed validation window, moves forward 12 months per time until exhausting the entire data length. Thus, the out-of-sample contains the full testing period, and it has 9 years with one update per year. Figure~\ref{fig:data_des1} shows the mechanism of the extensive window method in this chapter. \\

\section[Models for Chapter 2]{Models}\label{sec:models_ch2}
To begin this section, we will introduce the general additive prediction error model commonly used for asset pricing assignment:
\begin{equation}
r_{i,t+1} = \mathbb{E}_t \left[ r_{i,t+1} \right] + \varepsilon_{i,t+1}
\label{eq:return2.4}
\end{equation}
Where $r_{i,t+1}$ is the $r_{i,t+1}$ as asset excess returns at time t+1 with the assumption that $E_t[r_{i,t+1}]=0$ for $t\in[1,T-1]$,$i\in[1,N]$, $N$ is the number of assets. Concerning the work of GKX2020 \citep{Gu2020EmpiricalLearning}, the conditional expectation of $r_{i,t+1}$ can also be expressed as a function of a vector $f_{i,t}$ which is generated from encompassed P features (factors). $f_{i,t}$ can be directly equal to the factors if the number of factors is small and suited for linear models, but if the number of factors is large, such as the ‘factor zoo’ issue \citep{Harvey2019AZoo}, the additional process as principal components analysis (PCA) is required for shrinking the dimension of factors. This process is also known as ‘feature engineering or abstracting’ in ML terminology. Equation~\eqref{eq:return2.5} gives the general idea of a factor model. The earliest literature on asset pricing normally uses the ordinary least squares (OLS) linear form with less than 10 factors, but later, other function forms are applied due to the increasing factor numbers. In this chapter, Equation~\eqref{eq:return2.5} is implemented with an MLP function form.
\begin{equation}
r_{i,t+1} = g\left(f_{i,t}; \theta\right) + \varepsilon_{i,t+1}
\label{eq:return2.5}
\end{equation}
\subsection[Models for Chapter 2]{Multilayer Perceptron Algorithms (MLPs)}
\label{subsec:MLPs_ch2}
From Equation~\eqref{eq:return2.5}, it is clear that the function form is variable for adapting the factors. In this chapter, we employ the MLP model with a pyramid structure as a substitution for the traditional linear form of the factor model. The mechanism of MLP will be presented with an example, while the application of the factor model for asset pricing will be explained in line with the work of GKX2020. \\

Influenced by biological brain working mechanisms, vanilla neural network algorithms (alternatively multilayer perceptron) were developed in the 1960s, and a multitude of literature contributed to developing the modern concept of MLPs \citep{Rosenbaltt1957TheAutomation,Rumelhart1986LearningErrors,Werbos1974BeyondSciences}. A complete simple MLP structure constitutes one input layer, one or more hidden layers and one output layer. Each layer contains nodes, which are also known as neurons. Neurons are linked with other neurons from the layers next to them. Figure~\ref{fig:MLPs1_ch2} demonstrates the fully connected MLPs with and without hidden layers. 
\begin{figure}[htbp!]
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.9\columnwidth]{figs/MLPs1.png}
\end{center}
\caption[MLPs with (right) and without (left) hidden layers.]{MLPs with (right panel) and without (left panel) hidden layers. $\theta$ are the weight parameters and the $x_1,x_2,…,x_5$ are values calculated from an activation function $f(\cdot)$}
\label{fig:MLPs1_ch2}
\end{figure}
The left panel of Figure~\ref{fig:MLPs1_ch2} exhibits the MLP without a hidden layer. It can be as simple as a linear model. For the convenience of understanding the mathematical expression of MLP for the factor model, I  transform the fundamental factor model into:
\begin{equation}
r_{i,t+1} = \mathbb{E}_t \left( \beta f_t \right) + \varepsilon_{i,t+1}
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}_t \left( \beta f_t \right) = g\left( z_{i,t} \right)
\end{equation}
Where $g(\cdot)$ is a function form for mapping the factors to the excess returns $r_{i,t+1}, z_{i,t}$ is the dimensional vector of predictors (or features) transformed from the factors. Thus, the left panel of Figure~\ref{fig:MLPs1_ch2} as a linear model can be presented as:
\begin{equation}
g(z_i) = \theta_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{4} z_k \theta_{k}
\end{equation}
With the $\theta_0$ as the intercept and $\theta_k$ as the parameters for the features $z_k$. As the example shown in the left panel of Figure~\ref{fig:MLPs1_ch2}, if the input features only encompassed 4 dimensions, and all features have no correlation with each other, also, there is no collinearity among $z_k$, this could be ideal for modelling $r_{i,t+1}$. Nonetheless, when the dimension of $z_k$ increase, the risk of model misspecification will increase due to multi-collinearity, sample size and so on. Wherefore, the MLP proposes a possible non-linear function form of $g(z_{i,t})$ which is shown in the right panel of Figure~\ref{fig:MLPs1_ch2}.\\

The right panel of Figure~\ref{fig:MLPs1_ch2} gives an example of a feedforward MLP structure with 1 hidden layer containing 4 neurons. The structure contains 4 neurons in the input layer for the 4-dimension features $(z_1,…,z_4)$ and 1 node for the output $r_i$. Each node of the hidden layer can be seen as a linear model with a non-linear activation function, such that,
\begin{align}
x^{(1)}_1 &= f\left( \theta^{(0)}_{1,0} + \sum_{j=1}^{4} z_j \theta^{(0)}_{1,j} \right) \\
x^{(1)}_2 &= f\left( \theta^{(0)}_{2,0} + \sum_{j=1}^{4} z_j \theta^{(0)}_{2,j} \right) \\
&\vdots \notag \\
x^{(1)}_5 &= f\left( \theta^{(0)}_{5,0} + \sum_{j=1}^{4} z_j \theta^{(0)}_{5,j} \right)
\end{align}
Where $f(\cdot)$ is the activation function, $x_n^{(1)}$,$n=1,2,3,…$, is the $n_{th}$ neuron in the hidden layer, $\theta_{i,0}^{(0)},i=1,2,3,4,5$ are also named ‘bias’ and $\theta_{i,j}^{(0)}$ are also named ‘weights’. The number in parentheses is denoted as the number of hidden layers, in which case, it is ‘1’ in the right panel of Figure~\ref{fig:MLPs1_ch2}. From the hidden layer to the output layer, it is a linear model containing the $x_i$ as the predictors and $r_i$ as the response is shown in Equation~\eqref{eq:MLPs2.12}, where $\theta_0^{(1)}$,$\theta_n^{(1)}$ are the bias and weights respectively for the hidden layer to the output layer. 
\begin{equation}
g(z_i; \boldsymbol{\theta}) = \theta^{(1)}_0 + \sum_{n=1}^{5} x^{(1)}_n \theta^{(1)}_n
\label{eq:MLPs2.12}
\end{equation}
More generally, the MLP structure with h hidden layers and $n$ nodes in each layer, which contains $j$ features in the input layer and one output node, can be rewritten as Equation~\eqref{eq:input-layer_ch2} to Equation~\eqref{eq:output-layer_ch2}
\begin{align}
x^{(1)}_k &= f\left( \theta^{(I)}_{k,0} + \sum_{k=1}^{n} z_k \theta^{(I)}_k \right) \label{eq:input-layer_ch2} \\
x^{(h)}_k &= f\left( \theta^{(h)}_{k,0} + \sum_{k=1}^{n} x^{(h-1)}_k \theta^{(h)}_k \right) \label{eq:hidden-layer_ch2} \\
g(z_i; \boldsymbol{\theta}) &= \theta^{(O)}_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{n} x^{(h)}_k \theta^{(O)}_k \label{eq:output-layer_ch2}
\end{align}
Where $\theta_{n,0}^{(I)}$,$\theta_{n,0}^{(h)}$,$\theta_{n,0}^{(O)}$ are biased in input, hidden and output layers respectively, while $\theta_k^{(I)}$,$\theta_k^{(h)}$,$\theta_k^{(O)}$ are the weights in the input, hidden and output layers respectively. According to Equation~\eqref{eq:input-layer_ch2} to Equation~\eqref{eq:output-layer_ch2}, we derive:
\begin{equation}
g(z_i; \boldsymbol{\theta}_{n,0}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{k}) = \theta^{(O)}_0 + f^{(1)} f^{(2)} \dots f^{(h)} \left( z_i^\prime \boldsymbol{\theta}_k + \boldsymbol{\theta}_{n,0} \right)
\label{eq:gztt_ch2}
\end{equation}
Before passing the linear results to the next layer, a function is introduced to respond to the non-linearity which is named the activation function. Activation functions improve the flexibility of the general function form which increases the adaptability of complex feature structures. For the activation function $f(\cdot)$, modern NN theory recommends a rectified linear unit (ReLU) function \citep{Goodfellow2016DeepLearning}. with consideration of computational cost and forecasting accuracy, which is also widely used by empirical research in different domains. The activation function of ReLU is shown as simple as:
\begin{align}
ReLU(x) = \max\{0, x\}\\
ReLU(x) =
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } x < 0 \\
x & \text{if } x \geq 0
\end{cases}
\end{align}
Thus,
\begin{equation}
x^{(h)} = \mathrm{ReLU}\left( \boldsymbol{\Theta}^{(h)}_0 + \left(x^{(h-1)}\right)^\prime \boldsymbol{\Theta}^{(h)}_k \right)
\end{equation}
By following the work of GKX2020, the pyramid structure is applied in this chapter, which follows the sequence that:
\begin{equation}
\text{input dimension} > h_1 > h_2 > \cdots > \text{output dimension}
\end{equation}
Where the input dimension is equal to the feature’s number, $h(i),i=1,2,3…$ indicates the dimension of hidden layers. The output dimension is the number of output dimensions. GKX2020 simply used a fixed pyramid structure with $h_1 =32, h_2=16, h_3=8, h_4=4, h_5=2$ as suggested by \citet{Masters1993PracticalC++}. However, the fixed structure may not be adaptive for the variable input dimensions, and \citet{Coqueret2020MachineVersion} proposed a dynamic pyramid structure design method for MLP, which is:
\begin{equation}
U_k \approx \left\lfloor O\left( \frac{l}{0} \right)^{\frac{L+1-k}{L+1}} \right\rfloor
\end{equation}
Where $I$ is the input dimension,$L$ is the hidden layer numbers. $U_k$ is the dimension of the hidden layer $k$ and $O$ is the output dimension. It provides a structure with a more reasonable shrinkage of input features. Our MLP models implement the \citet{Coqueret2020MachineVersion}’s method for constructing the pyramid structure with the output dimension of one implies one stock’s excess return series. The inputs are factors derived from firm characteristic- sorted portfolios,  and one factor counts as one dimension.
\subsection[Models]{Loss Function and Model Estimation}
\label{subsec:lossEst_ch2}
The loss function is a function for measuring the predicted values and actual values, which scale the model performance. In ML literature, the Mean Squared Error (MSE) function is typically used for optimizing and estimating the regression model’s parameters. Equation~\eqref{eq:MSE_ch2} shows the MSE loss function and Equation~\eqref{eq:MSEEST_ch2} shows by minimizing the MSE, the model is updating with the optimized parameters for later forecasting tasks. The $r_{i,t}$ is the stock $i$’s actual excess return series, $g(z_{j,t}; \boldsymbol{\theta}_{n,0}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_k)$ is the estimated excess return from Equation~\eqref{eq:gztt_ch2}, $T$ is the observation numbers of excess returns or estimated excess returns.
\begin{equation}
MSE = \mathcal{L}\left(r_{i,t}, g(z_{j,t}; \boldsymbol{\theta}_{n,0}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_k)\right)
= \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \left( r_{i,t} - g(z_{j,t}; \boldsymbol{\theta}_{n,0}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_k) \right)^2
\label{eq:MSE_ch2}
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}\left( r_{i,t}, g(z_{j,t}; \boldsymbol{\theta}_{n,0}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_k) \right)
\label{eq:MSEEST_ch2}
\end{equation}
Unlike traditional statistic models such as OLS, which only split data as in-sample and out-of-sample (OOS), ML models add a validation period to relax the assumptions such as linearity or homoscedasticity of the traditional statistic models. Typically, people utilize gradient descent (GD) to search for the optimal parameters of the MLP models and examine them on the validation data. The best parameters with the lowest validation MSE will be adopted for the forecasting task on testing data. Equation~\eqref{eq:gra_ch2} and Equation~\eqref{eq:sgd_ch2} shows the GD process, where $\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ gradient, it is the partial derivative of the loss function and the individual model parameter, $\theta$ are the model parameters. $\varphi$ is the pre-set hyperparameter named learning rate, which determines how fast or accurate to find the parameters that let the loss function reach the global minimum. Normally, when $\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ is approaching zero, the loss function is considered as ‘reaching to the global minimum’.
\begin{align}
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = 
\left( 
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial \theta_1},\ 
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial \theta_2},\ 
\dots,\ 
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial \theta_n} 
\right)\label{eq:gra_ch2}\\
\boldsymbol{\theta} := \boldsymbol{\theta} - \varphi \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\label{eq:sgd_ch2}
\end{align}
Concerning the computational cost of ML algorithms, the most prevailing parameter searching process is the Stochastic GD (SGD) which updates parameters for each sample in each iteration. However, it introduces unexpected noise which could trigger the unstable convergence of the loss function. That is the reason for adding the optimizer of Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) \citep{Kingma2014Adam:Optimization} for stabilizing the SGD process. Adam introduced the first and second-moment estimation of gradients to achieve the acceleration of the loss function convergence and the self-adaptation of the learning rate. The pseudocode of Adam described in Appendix~\ref{sec:Algorithm Pseudocode}\\

The backpropagation algorithm is the algorithm for adjusting the weights in the network via calculating the gradient of the loss function with respect to each parameter from the output direction. It applies the “chain rule” of derivative computation to propagate gradients from the output layer backwards through the network. The process can be separated into five steps: obtaining results from forward propagation, computing the loss, backpropagation, updating weights, and iteration. Specifically, when the results are calculated from Equation~\eqref{eq:4.2.5_ch2} and Equation~\eqref{eq:4.2.6_ch2}, we derive the loss from the forward round. Here, $W^{(l)}$ is the weight matrix for the $l$-th layer, $b^{(l)}$ is the bias, $\sigma(\cdot)$ is the activation function, and $a^{(l-1)}$ is the activation from the previous layer.
\begin{align}
z^{(l)} = W^{(l)} a^{(l-1)} + b^{(l)}\label{eq:4.2.5_ch2}\\
a^{(l)} = \sigma\left( z^{(l)} \right)\label{eq:4.2.6_ch2}
\end{align}
After loss from the output layer $\sigma^{(L)}$ has computed via Equation~\eqref{eq:4.2.7_ch2}, backpropagation can take place. Here $L$ is the loss function.
\begin{equation}
\delta^{(L)} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{(L)}} \cdot \sigma'\left( z^{(L)} \right)
\label{eq:4.2.7_ch2}
\end{equation}
Concretely,
\begin{equation}
\delta^{(l)} = \left( \delta^{(l+1)} W^{(l+1)T} \right) \cdot \sigma'\left( z^{(l)} \right)
\label{eq:4.2.8_ch2}
\end{equation}
Where $W^{(l+1)T}$ is the transpose of the weight matrix of the $(l+1)$-th layer, $\sigma'\left( z^{(l)} \right)$ is the derivative of the activation function from the $l$-th layer. Then, the new gradients can be computed via:
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(l)}} = a^{(l-1)T} \delta^{(l)}\\
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)}
\end{align}
Eventually, the weights are updated via the GD process:
\begin{align}
W^{(l)} = W^{(l)} - \eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(l)}}\\
b^{(l)} = b^{(l)} - \eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(l)}}
\end{align}
\subsection[Models for Chapter 2]{Regularization}
\label{subsec:Regularization_ch2}
The ML models are common for adding regularizations which is an efficient approach for controlling the complexity of the models. As mentioned in GKX2020, they deployed the $l1$ regularization on the loss function. Equation~\eqref{eq:4.3.1_ch2} shows the $l1$ regularization. Where $\theta_j$ illustrates the individual estimated parameters and $\lambda$ is a hyperparameter that represents the regularization strength. The $l1$ norm could assist models to benefit from filtering the insignificant features by compressing the weights of these features to zero, which potentially increases the model interpretability and excludes the noise. Also, by controlling the overweighting, the $l1$ norm prevents model overfitting and improves the model's generalization capability. The penalty term of $\lambda \sum_{j=1}^{P} |\theta_j|$ is also known as the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO). In addition, the l1 regularization helps with correcting the direction of minimum MSE searching.
\begin{align}
MSE_{L_1} &= \mathcal{L}\left( r_{i,t}, g(z_{j,t}; \boldsymbol{\theta}_{n,0}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_k) \right) \notag \\
&= \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \left( r_{i,t} - g(z_{j,t}; \boldsymbol{\theta}_{n,0}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_k) \right)^2
+ \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{P} |\theta_j|
\label{eq:4.3.1_ch2}
\end{align}
\subsection[Models for Chapter 2]{Early Stopping and batch normalization}
\label{subsec:ESBN_ch2}
One parameter searching for all training data points in a batch is defined as one epoch. Epoch is a one-time gradient descent process. Normally, when the epoch number increases, the MSE of training and validation will decrease. However, as epochs are a hyperparameter of the MLP model, it is difficult to define before attempting the model. Oversize epochs will cause the overfitting issue as well because the difference of MSE for both training and validation data increases after epochs reach a critical minimum value. Early-stopping is a process for stopping the epochs when the performance on the validation data cannot be improved further, then logging the parameters for prediction. \\

Batch normalization is a vertical normalization, where each observation in the batch removes the batch’s mean and is divided by its standard deviation; the training data in one batch’s mean is zero, and the variance is equal to 1. Batch normalization can accelerate and stabilize the training process, moderate the issue of gradient vanishing and explosion \citep{Glorot2010UnderstandingNetworks}, which is explained in Section~\ref{subsec:gra_ve_ch2}, and reduce the sensitivity towards the initial weights.
\subsection[Models for Chapter 2]{Gradient vanishing and explosion}
\label{subsec:gra_ve_ch2}
Gradient vanishing usually happens during the backpropagation process. When the hidden layer number of the MLP model increased to a certain level, the gradient was extremely small or equal to zero. Subsequently, when it is passed back to the first hidden layer, the gradient vanishes, causing the parameters to pause updating, leading to poor performance of the model. This was especially prevalent when the activation function was using Sigmoid or Tanh. Whereas ReLU is the activation function which can prevent this issue since its derivative is most likely to be 1, batch normalization is another approach that also helps with this. Opposite to the scenario of gradient vanishing, if the initial learning rate is not properly set or an inappropriate depth to the MLP structure is deployed, the gradient could be extremely large. In that sense, if the learning rate causes excessively large parameter updating, the parameters do not converge the loss function to the global minimum but diverge from the global minimum.  This phenomenon is known as gradient explosion, and the loss function encountering gradient explosion tends to be infinite. Testing the initial learning rate and batch normalization can be applied as adjustment methods for this issue. 
\subsection[Models for Chapter 2]{Model performance evaluation}
\label{subsec:perform_evalu_ch2}
The performance is evaluated via the model interpretability indicator, coefficient of determination $R^2$, the out-of-sample $R$ square denoted as $R^2_{\text{oos}}$, and the model comparison test, the Diebold-Mariano (DM) Test \citep{Diebold1995ComRacy}. Also, variable importance, also known as feature importance, is measured via a permutation-based method \citep{Breiman2001RandomForests}. Equation~\eqref{eq:oosr2_4.6.1_ch2} presents the algorithm of $R^2_{\text{oos}}$. $r_{i,t+1}$ are the real out-of-sample excess returns, $\hat{r}_{i,t+1}$ is the predicted excess return, and $\bar{r}_{\text{train}}$ is the mean of the excess returns in the training period. $i$ indicates the stock $i$.
\begin{equation}
R^2_{\text{oos}} = 1 - \frac{\sum \left( r_{i,t+1} - \hat{r}_{i,t+1} \right)^2}
{\sum \left( r_{i,t+1} - \bar{r}_{\text{train}} \right)^2}
\label{eq:oosr2_4.6.1_ch2}
\end{equation}
The DM test is designed for model comparison. The mechanism of the DM test is to compare the forecasting errors between two models to show whether the difference is significantly different from zero. Equation~\eqref{eq:dm1_ch2} to Equation~\eqref{eq:dm3_ch2} show the algorithm of the DM test, where $|e^{(m)}_{i,t+1}|$, $|e^{(n)}_{i,t+1}|$ are the absolute forecasting errors derived from $(r_{i,t+1} - \hat{r}_{i,t+1})$ of model $m$ and $n$ respectively. $i$ indicates the stock $i$. $h$ is the number of stocks, which is 420 in this case. $d_{t+1}$ is the cross-sectional average difference between model $m$ and model $n$’s absolute forecasting errors, $\bar{d}$ is the mean of $d_{t+1}$, and $d_{\text{standard error}}$ is the standard error of $d_t$.
\begin{align}
d_{t+1} &= \frac{1}{h} \sum_{i=1}^{h} \left( \left| e^{(m)}_{i,t+1} \right| - \left| e^{(n)}_{i,t+1} \right| \right)\label{eq:dm1_ch2} \\
\bar{d} &= \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} d_{t+1}\label{eq:dm2_ch2} \\
DM_{\text{statistics}} &= \frac{\bar{d}}{d_{\text{standard error}}}\label{eq:dm3_ch2}
\end{align}
Variable importance is a technique commonly applied to ML, linear, and non-linear statistical models for verifying the impact of individual features. It gauges the level of increase or decrease in the forecasting errors when a feature’s value varies or is removed. The feature causes a large variation of forecasting error considered as important \citep{Breiman2001RandomForests}. The indicator is presented as a feature rank form for exhibiting the most important features to less important features. Equation~\eqref{eq:perm1_ch2} to Equation~\eqref{eq:perm3_ch2} exhibit the process of calculating the feature importance, where $L_{baseline}$ is baseline loss or original out-of-sample loss, $X$ is the original feature matrix, and $f(\cdot)$ is the model forms. $L_{perm(X_i)}$ is the loss that an individual feature $X_i$ is permutated. Then, the importance of $X_i$ is equal to the difference between the permutated loss and the baseline loss. 
\begin{align}
L_{\text{baseline}} &= \mathcal{L}(r_{i,t}, f(X)) \label{eq:perm1_ch2} \\
L_{\text{perm}}(X_i) &= \mathcal{L}(r_{i,t}, f(X_{\text{perm}})) \label{eq:perm2_ch2} \\
\text{Importance}(X_i) &= L_{\text{perm}}(X_i) - L_{\text{baseline}} \label{eq:perm3_ch2}
\end{align}

A common trading signal detection technique is applied to forecast the excess returns of each stock, and all these stocks are organized as an equal-weight portfolio. The strategy is the single-sided positive strategy that if the sign of the actual excess return and predicted excess return are both positive, then long the stock from the next value. This is denoted as the ‘open a long position’. Afterwards, if the actual excess return and predicted excess return are both negative, close the long position by selling the stock. Concerning the unstable borrowing rates in stock trading practice, to prevent the systematic risks brought by the extreme cases, the back test of this chapter excludes the short trading option (negative signal for opening then positive for closing the positions). The transaction cost is taken as an average value from the existing literature \citep{Ma2023AttentionApproach}, which is 50 basis points. The transaction cost (TC) takes into the proportional wise, can be written as:
\begin{equation}
TC = \text{returns} \times 50~\text{basis points}
\end{equation}
The portfolio performances of distinctive models are evaluated using the indicators of Jensen’s alpha \citep{Jensen1968The1945-1964}, annualised returns, Sharpe ratio (SR), Sortino ratio (SO), maximum drawdown (MDD), and standard deviation (Std). These indicators are compared across two periods: before and including the pandemic. Specifically, Equation~\eqref{eq:alpha5.1_ch2} presents the calculation of Jensen’s alpha, defined as the difference between the expected out-of-sample excess returns and the expected predicted excess returns. It reflects the performance of the overall trading strategy (including the designed models), showing how much gain exceeds what is explained by the factors. The formula for annualised return is given in Equation~\eqref{eq:annualized_return5.2_ch2}, which applies monthly compounding to cumulative returns. The Sharpe ratio and Sortino ratio are presented in Equations~\eqref{eq:sharpe_ratio5.3_ch2} and \eqref{eq:sortino_ratio5.4_ch2}, where $E(r_p)$ is the expected portfolio return, $r_f$ is the risk-free rate, $\sigma_p$ is the standard deviation of portfolio returns, and $\sigma_d$ is the downside deviation. The maximum drawdown (MDD), shown in Equation~\eqref{eq:mdd5.5_ch2}, is a crucial risk measurement that indicates the largest peak-to-trough decline in portfolio excess returns. Here, $C_{\max}(t)$ denotes the maximum cumulative value up to time $t$, and $C(t)$ is the value at time $t$.
\begin{align}
\alpha_i &= \mathbb{E}(r_{i,t}) - \mathbb{E}(\hat{r}_{i,t}) \label{eq:alpha5.1_ch2} \\
AR &= \left\{ 1 + \left[ \prod_{i=1}^{n} (1 + r_{i,t}) - 1 \right]^{\frac{12}{n}} \right\} - 1 \label{eq:annualized_return5.2_ch2} \\
SR &= \frac{\mathbb{E}(r_p) - r_f}{\sigma_p} \label{eq:sharpe_ratio5.3_ch2} \\
SO &= \frac{\mathbb{E}(r_p) - r_f}{\sigma_d} \label{eq:sortino_ratio5.4_ch2} \\
\text{MDD} &= \max_{t \in [0, T]} \left( \frac{C_{\max}(t) - C(t)}{C_{\max}(t)} \right) \label{eq:mdd5.5_ch2}
\end{align}
Eventually, the results are compared both internally and externally. Internally, we compare the indicators of different models. Externally, it attempts to seek the overall trading strategy performance with and without the impact of COVID-19.

For understanding which features or factors are most important for the proposed models, variable importance examination usually plays an important role. As presented in Section 4, the permutation-based variable importance testing is applied to the proposed MLP models. It shows that factors have different importance in different models over time. To explore how they change, the variable importance for the full testing period ('2112'), pre-COVID('1911') and 1-year post-COVID period ('2212') are examined, which is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:iv_2112_ch2} to 5.2.6 respectively. Interestingly, examining all periods closely agrees that the factors of Announcement Return (AnnouncementReturn) and Earnings Forecast Disparity (EarningsForecastDisparity) have the highest influence in all models for all examined periods. They are followed by size (size), Book Leverage (BookLeverage), earning forecast revision (REV6), idiosyncratic risk with Fama French 3 factors (IdioVol3F), EPS forecast revision (AnalystRevision) and industry momentum (IndMom). It partly confirms the original results of GKX2020’s MLP models. By jointly considering the variable importance and OOS $R^2$, the MLP models have no myth of ‘deeper, better’ due to the limitation of data size. It proves the point given by \citet{Coqueret2020MachineVersion} that the higher the data size to parameters size ratio, the lower the overfitting risks. The proposed MLP model as an example, the OOS $R^2$ values decrease from MLP with 2 hidden layers. When the hidden layer number increases to 5, it shows the overfitting tendency and the OOS interpretability seems to disappear. Similar to the OOS $R^2$ indicator, the variable importance testing results imply the fading trend when the number of hidden layers increases as well.\\

Figure~\ref{fig:iv_2112_ch2} presents the top 20 important factors of each model for the full testing period, and it illustrates that Model fw1 to fw5 are in close agreement concerning the most influential factors. Apart from the aforementioned crucial factors, the stock excess returns in the selected dataset are highly driven by earnings surprise of big firms (EarnSupBig), return on equity (RoE), earnings streak length (NumEarnIncrease), Forecast \& Accrual (ChForecastAccrual), Decline in analyst coverage (ChNAnalyst), Payout Yield (PayoutYield) and  Net Payout Yield (NetPayoutYield). Model fw5 partially concurs with the results of Model fw1 to fw4, but it favours more momentum factors. For the best performing models, regarding OOS $R^2$, the fw2 has the Earnings Forecast Disparity, Announcement Return, Book Leverage, Size and Earnings Streak Length as the highest influential factors. Nevertheless, fw3 is quite different from fw2, which has idiosyncratic risk with Fama French 3 factors, size and Announcement Return as top 3 factors whose influence is significantly higher than the rest factors in the top 20 factors.\\

To summarize, the proposed MLP models with 2 hidden layers outperform all alternative models with the highest OOS $R^2$ value, which is followed by the one with 3 hidden layers. All proposed MLP models’ performance is significantly improved when the COVID-19 period data is counted in the testing period, but the benchmark models show less sensitivity to the pandemic effect. Except for the GKX2020 with 2 and 3 hidden layers, alternative models’ performances are different from each other at the 5\% significance level at least. Additionally, individual stock performance may have a significant impact on overall portfolio performance. Size, as one of the most important factors, has a crucial impact on all proposed models when the market faces extreme fluctuations, as well as momentum factors and the factor of ‘earnings surprise of big firms (EarnSupBig)’. The general fading variable importance in fw4 to fw5, together with results from OOS $R^2$, challenges the legend ‘deep, better’ of MLP models. \subsection[Empirical Application and Results for Chapter 2]{Evaluation of Back Testing Performance}
\label{subsec:back_testing_eva_ch2}
The portfolio performance is commonly evaluated via indicators such as annualised returns (annual return), Sharpe Ratio (SR), Sortino ratio (SO), maximum drawdown (MDD) and $\alpha$. Table~\ref{tab:EW_ch2} shows the equal-weighted portfolios’ performance of the selected 420 stocks with and without the pandemic period. The overall annual return is clearly higher when the pandemic period is included, and the annual return for individual models shows the same tendency. Although the overall standard deviation (Std) is higher for the full period of testing, it does not affect the annual return much. For both periods tested, the lowest annual returns are from the models of ‘MLP\_fw1’, ‘ols’,’pls’ and ‘pcr’, and the rest of MLP based models, show a trend of ‘deeper, better’, but interestingly, none of them gains higher excess returns compared with the ‘buy-and-hold’ strategy. Also, for the proposed models, a deeper structure comes with the higher Std, but the highest Std is shown by the ‘buy-and-hold’ strategy. Sharpe ratios reflect the capital gain under a certain level of risk which is measured by the standard deviation of excess returns. The full testing period’s performance on SR is better than the COVID testing period. All models in the full testing period are higher than or very close to the benchmark of ‘buy-and-hold’. However, during the pre-COVID period, all models were lower than or extremely close to ‘buy-and-hold’. An analogous phenomenon appears on SO as well, which scales the gain from downside risks (e.g. the standard deviation from the negative excess returns). MDD, which measures the largest downfall from peak to the bottom of portfolio excess returns, shows the opposite trends to SR and SO, all lower than ‘buy-and-hold’ in the full period but higher in the pre-pandemic period. During the full period of testing, our best-performing model, MLP with 2 hidden layers, showed a great advantage which achieving the SR of 0.2651, Sortino Ratio of 0.4154 and the lowest MDD of 39.03\% followed by MLP with 3 hidden layers. This model beat the traditional statistical models and the shallower MLP structure model as well. From the factor investing angle, alpha measures the extra gains from factors; all models have positive alphas, which are significant from zero for both periods. The proposed deep MLP models have higher alphas in the full testing period, but no higher than GKX2020’s MLP models. From the asset pricing theory perspective, lower alpha indicates a better excess return explainability of the factors; ideally, it could be insignificant. Thus, the MLP with 1 hidden layer achieved the best interpretability for the labels in the full period. From a factor investing perspective, practitioners prefer a higher alpha, which implies their trading strategy is ‘beating the factors’; hence, the GKX2020 model with 4 hidden layers may satisfy their needs. Noticeably, the performance of GKX2020 models on the proposed dataset exhibits the similarity and approach to the ‘buy-and-hold’ strategy, which is detected as the trading signal capture failing. \\

As shown in the pre-COVID testing period, the results have a mild upward tendency. The overall annual return is around 2\% lower than the full testing period. The Std is around 0.01 lower as well. Shape Ratio and Sortino Ratio present that the proposed MLP models have a ‘deep, better’ trend, better than the ‘ols’, ‘pls’ and ‘pcr’ models, but the difference between SR and SO is less significant than the ones in the full testing period. It implies that models suffered higher downside risks in the pre-COVID period than in the pandemic period. The lowest MDD shows in the MLP with 3 hidden layers, but the best SR and SO appear in the MLP with 5 hidden layers, which also has the lowest alpha value. However, the ‘fw5’ and GKX2020 models’ performance approaches the ‘buy-and-hold’ benchmark, which implies the failure to detect sign-based trading signals. The ‘ols’, ‘pls’ and ‘pcr’ models achieve similar but better alphas in the pre-COVID period, which implies that practitioners have extra gain from the factor investing. Their alphas are even higher than the best alpha in the full testing period, which implies that, without high market fluctuation, the simplest models may lead to a greater gain from factors. But anyway, by comparing the full testing period and pre-COVID testing period results, it shows that the best proposed MLP models have higher profitability with relatively low risks. Figure~\ref{fig:EW_cumulative_ch2} illustrates the cumulative excess returns of all models for the full testing period. It clearly shows our best-proposed model well managed the downside risks and gained a relatively high excess return for the equal-weighted portfolio, no matter the testing period including or excluding the pandemic albeit the returns derived all less than the simplest ‘buy-and-hold’ strategy.\\

Apart from the equal-weighted portfolios, the valued weighted method is widely used for portfolio strategy-wise evaluation. As early as \citet{Fama1993CommonBonds} to later GKX2020 \citep{Gu2020EmpiricalLearning}, all factor models have employed the value-weighted method. Specifically, value weights are generated from the ratio of an individual stock’s market capital to the total market capital of all selected stocks. The portfolio returns are generated by the weighted average of the individual stocks. Table~\ref{tab:VW_ch2} is the report of the value-weighted portfolio organised by the selected 420 large capital stocks. It contains two parts as the equal-weighted portfolio reports, which are the full testing period and the testing period with COVID-19 excluded. Since model-wise extra gain alpha is never affected by weights, the value-weighted portfolio’s alpha is equal to the equal-weighted portfolio’s alpha, thus, Table~\ref{tab:VW_ch2} does not repetitively report alpha.\\

With the full testing period, the conclusions drawn from the equal-weighted portfolio still hold for the value-weighted portfolio. From the table, the annual returns of all models are quite similar to the equal-weighted portfolio’s annual returns, but standard deviations are lower than the equal-weighted portfolio’s. The Sharpe Ratios are relatively higher, but the Sortino Ratios are varying among models. The differences in Sortino Ratio between individual models are less pronounced when compared with equal-weighted portfolio’s Sortino Ratios. The overall maximum drawdowns are dropped considerably, and the highest Sortino Ratio value shows up on the proposed MLP model with 3 hidden layers which comes with the second lowest MDD (33.04\%). Compared to the lowest MDD in the equal-weighted portfolio with the full testing period, it dropped 15.37\%. This implies that the value-weighted portfolio moderates the downside risks with a reasonable gain in the full testing period. Figure~\ref{fig:VW_cumulative_ch2} also shows how the value-weighted portfolio moderates the downside risks. Figure~\ref{fig:VW_cumulative_ch2} presents the full testing period cumulative returns of all models. It exhibits clearly that MLP with 3 hidden layers (green line) well reduced the downside fluctuation with a decent gain. Signal-detecting failure still exists in the deep MLP model and GKX2020 models. \\

In the pre-COVID testing period, compared with the equal-weighted portfolio, the annual returns for all models are slightly higher than annual returns in the equal-weighted portfolio and the Std is noticeably decreased for MLP-based models including GKX2020, but no great change in ‘ols’, ‘pls’ and ‘pcr’ models. The lowest MDD took place at MLP with 3 hidden layers which is 26.50\%, but the proposed MLP model with the highest SR and SO cannot surpass the ‘buy-and-hold’ strategy. Whereas the overall SOs are higher than the ones in the equal-weighted portfolio at the same period settings. The SR and SO of proposed MLP models show a ‘deeper, higher’ trend. Since portfolio weighting has no impact on signal detecting, the GKX2020 and deep MLP model signal detecting failure still exist under the value weighting mode in both periods. From Figure~\ref{fig:VW_cumulative_ch2} the optimal option for a sign-based trading strategy on the value-weighted portfolio is the proposed MLP model with 3 hidden layers which are denoted as ‘fw3’.

In conclusion, no matter whether the equal-weighted portfolio or the value-weighted portfolio, the overall annual returns from the full testing period perform better than the period without the pandemic due to the strong rebound trend during the pandemic. The strong upward trend, which is beyond the level of crash caused by the pandemic, increases the SR and SO as well. The standard deviations for all models are smaller in the pre-pandemic period, while the MDDs are generally smaller in the pandemic as well. Between the equal-weighted portfolio and value-weighted portfolio, the value-weighted portfolio for the full testing period performs well for moderating the downside risks, while for the pre-pandemic period, it increases the capital gain under certain risks for all models. Among the main and benchmark models, all proposed MLP models outperform the traditional statistic models as OLS, PLS and PCR under all scenarios. By considering risks and returns, the proposed MLP model with 3 hidden layers outperforms under the circumstances of the value-weighted portfolio for both periods and the equal-weighted portfolio for the pre-pandemic period. It well managed the balance of downside risk and relatively large capital gain, but for the equal-weighted portfolio full testing period, the MLP with 2 hidden layers overtakes alternative model, achieving a better gain relative to its risks. All models in all scenarios have significant positive OOS alphas, which indicates the extra gain from factors. However,  GKX2020 models in all scenarios fail to detect trading signals. Their performance approaches the performance of the ‘buy-and-hold’ strategy. The main findings in this section are presented as: firstly, the model overfitting issue traps the sign-based trading signal detection; secondly, when the market experiences a strong upward trend, the fundamental trading strategy such as ‘buy-and-hold’ could be the most efficient trading strategy without considering the risks. In this sense, MLP models’ meaning for factor investing is more about managing downside risks and deriving a relatively high return instead of ‘beating the market’. Finally, the value-weighted portfolio optimizes downside risks compared to the equal-weighted portfolio. Finally, trading signal filtering techniques can be applied to the system to further optimize the profitability and risks.

\section[Conclusion for Chapter 2]{Conclusion and Discussion}\label{sec:conclusion_ch2}
This chapter revisits and develops the GKX2020’s MLP models amid employing a dynamic MLP structure introduced by \citet{Coqueret2020MachineVersion} and features as firm characteristics sorted factors provided by \citet{AndrewY.Zimmermann2020OpenPricing}, re-evaluating the model and portfolio performance during the testing period of COVID-19, restricting the stocks with consideration of more realistic US stock markets conditions such as high liquidity, ‘going concern’, variable borrowing rates and available borrowing shares from the brokers. Similar to the findings in the original work of GKX2020, with data length limitation, the MLP models have no ‘deeper, better’ performance. It does not like the applications in computer vision, speech recognition and biological engineering which contain sufficient data length, but GKX2020’s MLP models more rely on the depth of the structure.  The MLP models’ performance on our dataset peaked at MLP with 2 hidden layers and faded after MLP with 3 hidden layers. As discussed in GKX2020, data size is a great challenge in ML-based factor modelling. However, the proposed MLP models have a better OOS fitness than GKX2020’s work. In addition, the firm characteristic-sorted factors compared with firm characteristics as observable factors are more accessible and stable for MLP model training in factor modelling. The most powerful predictor in all proposed MLP models is size followed by Earnings forecast revisions (REV6), Earnings announcement return (AnnouncementReturn), and Cash flow to market (CF) on our data settings which matched the findings from the original paper of GKX2020. Albeit, the long-only setting portfolio has lower Sharpe ratios and Sortino ratios than the two-way portfolio, it is more practicable for factor investors from the systematic risk management perspective. Our best-performed models achieve a great balance on the investing profitability and market fluctuation risks whether the COVID-19 period is applied. \\

Our work also verified the GKX2020’s notion that MLP models without signal filtering mechanisms would be highly affected by the market timing noises and found that MLP models which suffer from serious overfitting fail to capture the trading signals. The investing performance can be improved by finding the solutions for these market timing challenges such as adding a signal filtering mechanism. The MLP models in our case have considerable meanings in moderating the downside risks with the relatively highest gain, which verified the results from \citet{Avramov2021MachinePredictability}, rather than achieving the absolute annual returns when experiencing the steep increasing trend which covers the drawdowns caused by events with medium-term effects. In this sense, apart from the signal filtering, the stock selection has a high impact on portfolio performance as well. All models examined have significant $\alpha$ to some extent which indicates the profitability from factors. \\

Overall, MLP models bring promising performance on downside risk control and relatively high annual return after transaction cost for factor investing in all scenarios of our case, especially during the COVID-19 period. The design of ours highly approached the real practicable conditions which makes it more applicable to the market practitioners. It highlights the untility of new inspirations on neural network models on the asset pricing assignment for both industrial applications and academic research. Whereas, the existing challenges of limited data length, trading signal filtering, model hyperparameters tuning and stock selection which highly influence the model and portfolio performance. Topics such as how to moderate the restriction of data length, improve the trading signal quality and tune the model hyperparameter effectively are still worth further exploration. \\

\begin{appendices}

\section{Algorithm Pseudocode}\label{sec:Algorithm Pseudocode}

\subsection{Adam optimizer}\label{subsec:Adam optimizer}
Adam updates parameters by maintaining the first and second moments of the gradients.
\begin{algorithm}[H]
\caption{Adam Optimization}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\State \textbf{Initialize:} $m_0 = 0$, $v_0 = 0$, $l = 0$
\State \textbf{Set hyperparameters:} learning rate $\eta = 0.001$, $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.999$, $\epsilon = 10^{-8}$
\While{$\theta_l$ not converged}
    \State $l \gets l + 1$
    \State Compute gradient: $g_l = \nabla_\theta L(\theta_{l-1})$
    \State $m_l \gets \beta_1 m_{l-1} + (1 - \beta_1) g_l$
    \State $v_l \gets \beta_2 v_{l-1} + (1 - \beta_2) g_l \odot g_l$ \Comment{$\odot$: element-wise multiplication}
    \State $\hat{m}_l \gets \frac{m_l}{1 - \beta_1^l}$ \Comment{Bias correction}
    \State $\hat{v}_l \gets \frac{v_l}{1 - \beta_2^l}$
    \State $\theta_l \gets \theta_{l-1} - \eta \cdot \frac{\hat{m}_l}{\sqrt{\hat{v}_l} + \epsilon}$
\EndWhile
\State \textbf{Return:} $\theta_l$
\end{algorithmic}
\begin{flushleft}
\textit{Source: Adapted from \citet{Gu2020EmpiricalLearning}}
\end{flushleft}
\end{algorithm}
where $g_t$ and $\theta_t$ represent the gradients and parameters computed from previous sections respectively.
\subsection{Early stopping}\label{subsec:Early stopping}
\begin{algorithm}[H]
\caption{Early Stopping}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\State \textbf{Initialize:} $j = 0$, $\epsilon = \infty$, select patience parameter $p$.
\While{$j < p$}
    \State Update $\theta$ using the training algorithm (e.g., for $h$ steps).
    \State Calculate the prediction error from the validation sample, denoted as $\epsilon'$.
    \If{$\epsilon' < \epsilon$}
        \State $j \gets 0$
        \State $\epsilon \gets \epsilon'$
        \State $\theta' \gets \theta$
    \Else
        \State $j \gets j + 1$
    \EndIf
\EndWhile
\State \textbf{Return:} $\theta'$
\end{algorithmic}
\begin{flushleft}
\textit{Source: Adapted from \citet{Gu2020EmpiricalLearning}}
\end{flushleft}
\end{algorithm}

title: The Mechanism of Shrimpoluminescence
summary:
Snapping shrimp produce bubbles that emit light when they collapse. When a
bubble collapses so strongly that it emits light, the light emission is usually
called sonoluminescence; in the case of the shrimp, it is called
"shrimpoluminescence". The bubble collapses so fast that no heat can escape and
the gas trapped in the bubble becomes hot enough to ionize. Light is emitted
through electron-ion bremsstrahlung, electron-atom bremsstrahlung, and
electron-ion recombination. In this paper, we study the dynamics of a
sonoluminescing bubble and learn how to calculate the spectrum of emitted
light, allowing us to explain the physical mechanisms of shrimpoluminescence.

title: Purcell enhancement of photogalvanic currents in a van der Waals plasmonic self-cavity
summary:
Cavities provide a means to manipulate the optical and electronic responses
of quantum materials by selectively enhancing light-matter interaction at
specific frequencies and momenta. While cavities typically involve external
structures, exfoliated flakes of van der Waals (vdW) materials can form
intrinsic self-cavities due to their small finite dimensions, confining
electromagnetic fields into plasmonic cavity modes, characterized by
standing-wave current distributions. While cavity-enhanced phenomena are
well-studied at optical frequencies, the impact of self-cavities on nonlinear
electronic responses--such as photogalvanic currents--remains largely
unexplored, particularly in the terahertz regime, critical for emerging
ultrafast optoelectronic technologies. Here, we report a self-cavity-induced
Purcell enhancement of photogalvanic currents in the vdW semimetal WTe$_2$.
Using ultrafast optoelectronic circuitry, we measured coherent near-field THz
emission resulting from nonlinear photocurrents excited at the sample edges. We
observed enhanced emission at finite frequencies, tunable via excitation
fluence and sample geometry, which we attribute to plasmonic interference
effects controlled by the cavity boundaries. We developed an analytical theory
that captures the cavity resonance conditions and spectral response across
multiple devices. Our findings establish WTe$_2$ as a bias-free,
geometry-tunable THz emitter and demonstrate the potential of self-cavity
engineering for controlling nonlinear, nonequilibrium dynamics in quantum
materials.

title: Reversible Imprecise Markov Chains
summary:
Reversible Markov chains have identical forward and backward path
distributions; this symmetry yields tractable stationary behaviour and powers
algorithms from MCMC to network random-walk analysis. We extend reversibility
to imprecise Markov chains, in which marginal and transition probabilities are
specified by credal sets. Adopting the strong-independence interpretation of
the Markov property, we reverse every precise chain compatible with a given
credal specification and study the resulting ensemble. Because the reversed
ensemble generally cannot be encoded by the usual forward model - a credal
initial distribution pushed through a credal set of transition matrices - we
introduce a symmetric representation based on credal sets of two-step joint
distribution or edge-measure matrices. This framework is strictly more
expressive, admits a natural reversal operation, and reduces reversibility to
simple matrix symmetry. It also lets forward and reverse dynamics be described
simultaneously within one closed, convex set, paving the way for efficient
algorithms to evaluate expectations of path-dependent functionals. We
illustrate the theory with random walks on graphs and outline procedures for
computing lower expectations of path-based quantities.

\title{Reversible Imprecise Markov Chains}
\author{Damjan \v{S}kulj\\
	University of Ljubljana, Faculty of Social Sciences\\
	Kardeljeva pl. 5, SI-1000 Ljubljana, Slovenia\\
